e-4414.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of a Matrix
e-4414.worked_solution:
First, to find $A^2,$ we multiply $A$ by itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 10 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $A^4 = A^2 \cdot A^2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{4} & ={A}^{2}\cdot {A}^{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 10 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 10 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}81 & 0 \\ 100 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-4417.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the polynomial, interpreting any constants as multiples of the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(X) & =-{X}^{2}+3X+2 \\  & =-{X}^{2}+3X+2I\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find $f(D)=-D^2+3D+2I.$

Let's calculate $D^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =D\cdot D \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -10 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can evaluate $f(D)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(D) & =-{D}^{2}+3D+2I \\  & =-[\begin{aligned}1 & -10 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 10 \\ 0 & -9\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 & 15 \\ 0 & -9\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1+3+2 & 10+15+0 \\ 0 & -9-9+2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 25 \\ 0 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the polynomial, interpreting any constants as multiples of the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(X) & ={X}^{2}-2X-5 \\  & ={X}^{2}-2X-5I\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find $f(C)={C}^{2}-2C-5I.$

Let's calculate ${C}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can evaluate $f(C):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(C) & ={C}^{2}-2C-5I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 6 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7-2-5 & 4-4-0 \\ 6-6-0 & 7-2-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(X) & ={X}^{2}-2X-5 \\  & ={X}^{2}-2X-5I\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find $f(C)={C}^{2}-2C-5I.$

Let's calculate ${C}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can evaluate $f(C):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(C) & ={C}^{2}-2C-5I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 6 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7-2-5 & 4-4-0 \\ 6-6-0 & 7-2-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
